title: The Secret To Perfect Transitions In 5 Simple Steps -steps/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that the key to smooth classroom transitions isn't the destination activity but the standardized 'space between' activities, which can be replicated identically regardless of what students are transitioning to or from. He details a five-step sequence: signal for attention, use the phrase 'In a moment' to hold students' focus while directions are given, deliver precise directions, use a clear 'go' signal to release students into the transition, and observe closely without offering reminders or encouragement, sending students back to redo the transition if it falls short. Linsin frames this standardization as building students a dependable 'bridge' across the turbulent, unstructured moments between activities, arguing that lack of standardization—not the nature of any particular transition—is the chief reason classrooms struggle in this area.
points: The key insight is that the 'transition' itself—the space between activities—can be standardized and replicated regardless of the specific activities involved.
Step 1: signal for attention; Step 2: use the phrase 'In a moment' to hold focus while more directions follow.
Step 3: give precise, plain directions for what students should do; Step 4: use a clear 'go' signal to release students into the transition.
Step 5: observe closely without offering reminders or encouragement, sending students back to redo the transition if it isn't performed well.
Lack of standardization—not the specific destination or activity—is identified as the chief reason classrooms struggle with transitions.
quotes: Where students are going, or coming from, isn’t the transition. The transition is the space between.
If you standardize these brief moments, if you do the exact same thing regardless of where you’re transitioning to or coming from, they’ll be predictably smooth every time.
After waiting until every eye is on you, begin your directions with the words, “In a moment.” What this does is keep your students from moving on, mentally or otherwise, until you finish speaking.
Your only job now is to observe and verify that your directions are being carried out. Resist the urge to offer reminders or encouragement or otherwise interrupt them during the transition.
To make transitions efficient and devoid of misbehavior, you must build your students a bridge.
